new.question: A Ponzi scheme — named for Charles Ponzi's 1920 Boston fraud — pays earlier investors with newer investors' money. Bernie Madoff returned ~10% per year for 17+ years, regardless of market booms or crashes. What was the Ponzi tell?
new.answer: Consistent returns regardless of market conditions — mathematically impossible for any real strategy
choices: Consistent returns regardless of market conditions — mathematically impossible for any real strategy
Madoff's fees were lower than industry average — real fraudsters always overcharge investors heavily
Madoff's office building was small — real money managers always rent space in landmark towers
Madoff filed SEC paperwork on time — real fraudsters always skip the filing deadlines completely
new.context: Markopolos's 2005 memo: 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund is a Fraud.' Madoff confessed Dec 2008 once redemptions drained the cash. ~$65B paper / ~$19B real losses. The same mechanics as Charles Ponzi's 1920 Boston scheme — different decade, same flat-line tell.

rewrites.issue: Uses 'Ponzi tell' without teaching what a Ponzi scheme is — defines inline now

new.question: A Ponzi scheme — named for Charles Ponzi's 1920 Boston fraud — pays earlier investors with newer investors' money rather than from real profits. Lebanon's pound was pegged to the dollar at 1,507:1 from 1997. By late 2019 the central-bank Ponzi structure of Lebanese banking — paying high dollar interest from newer dollar deposits — became unsustainable. By 2023 the parallel rate was 100,000+ to the dollar; ~85% of Lebanon fell into poverty. What did the high-rate program depend on?
new.answer: Continuous new dollar inflow to pay old depositors — when inflows slowed, obligations failed; Ponzi mechanics at sovereign scale
choices: Continuous new dollar inflow to pay old depositors — when inflows slowed, obligations failed; Ponzi mechanics at sovereign scale
Genuine dollar-earning investments at real returns above 20% — the scheme was legitimate until politically destroyed by external sanctions
Direct US Federal Reserve subsidies to Lebanese banks — the dollar guarantee came from American taxpayer-funded Treasury backing programs
Lebanese oil revenue redirected to depositor interest — the country's hydrocarbon wealth covered the high-rate dollar program for two decades
new.context: Banque du Liban under governor Riad Salameh ran high-interest dollar accounts funded by newer dollar deposits. When Syrian refugees, remittances, and Gulf inflows slowed, the structure collapsed. Lebanese savings of a generation were wiped out. Salameh faced criminal investigation in multiple jurisdictions by 2023.

rewrites.issue: Uses 'Ponzi structure' to describe Lebanese banking without teaching mechanism — bumped to T5 to fit story-in-stem

new.question: A 'Credit Default Swap' (CDS) is insurance against a bond defaulting — buyer pays premiums; seller pays out if the bond fails. AIG was the world's largest insurer in 2008; its Financial Products division had sold ~$440B in CDS on mortgage securities with NO reserves. As mortgages crashed, AIG faced overwhelming margin calls. The Fed extended an $85B emergency loan Sept 16, 2008. Why did AIG's CDS exposure threaten the entire system?
new.answer: Every major bank had bought AIG-issued CDS protection — if AIG defaulted, banks worldwide would face simultaneous insurance failures; total federal commitments topped $182B
choices: Every major bank had bought AIG-issued CDS protection — if AIG defaulted, banks worldwide would face simultaneous insurance failures; total federal commitments topped $182B
AIG was the only US insurance company in 2008 — its failure would have eliminated all property and life insurance across the country for many years afterward
AIG held deeds to most American homes — its failure would have triggered automatic foreclosure on roughly 60% of US residential mortgages held by working families
AIG owned controlling stakes in every major bank — its failure would have liquidated the largest US banks via cross-shareholding, requiring federal takeover
new.context: AIG sold CDS without reserves because the senior tranches of mortgage securities were rated AAA — assumed never to fail. When housing collapsed, the 'impossible' losses hit. Goldman Sachs received $13B via AIG. The canonical 2008 moral-hazard moment.

rewrites.issue: Uses 'CDS' (credit default swap) without defining the term — many readers won't know

new.question: A Ponzi scheme (Charles Ponzi, Boston 1920) pays earlier investors with newer investors' money — no real profit. Lebanon's banking collapsed 2019-2020: Banque du Liban under governor Salameh ran an unsustainable currency peg AND a Ponzi-like dollar program — high dollar interest funded by newer dollar deposits. Pound (1,507/USD since 1997) collapsed to 100,000+/USD by 2023; ~85% poverty. What does this show about sovereign-level high-rate programs?
new.answer: Sovereign Ponzi mechanics are still Ponzi mechanics — when new inflows slow, the scheme collapses regardless of the central-bank stamp; a generation's savings vanish
choices: Sovereign Ponzi mechanics are still Ponzi mechanics — when new inflows slow, the scheme collapses regardless of the central-bank stamp; a generation's savings vanish
Sovereign dollar programs are inherently safe — central bank involvement guarantees full convertibility under all conditions, with no real depositor risk anywhere
Sovereign pegs always fail from external political pressure — the 2019-20 collapse was caused entirely by US sanctions and would not have happened otherwise
Sovereign banks face no liquidity risk — the IMF was legally required to backstop the Lebanese system and chose not to for unrelated political reasons
new.context: Salameh personally faced criminal investigation in multiple jurisdictions by 2023. The case is the canonical 21st-century example of central-bank-administered Ponzi mechanics — distinct from Madoff (private), but the same diagnostic.

rewrites.issue: Uses 'Ponzi-like dollar-deposit scheme' without teaching Ponzi mechanics

new.question: Roth IRA (after-tax contribution, tax-free withdrawal) and Traditional IRA (pre-tax contribution, taxed withdrawal) are the two main tax-advantaged retirement accounts. Roth IRAs phase out above ~$161,000 single in 2024 — high earners can't contribute directly. But they CAN contribute to a Traditional IRA (no income limit) and convert it to Roth the next day. The conversion is taxed but legal. What is this called?
new.answer: Backdoor Roth — a legal loophole high earners use to access Roth benefits Congress meant to deny them
choices: Backdoor Roth — a legal loophole high earners use to access Roth benefits Congress meant to deny them
Reverse rollover — a tax penalty Congress imposes on workers who try to convert retirement accounts mid-stream
Pro-rata adjustment — an IRS-mandated procedure that erases any tax advantage from the conversion process
Phase-out conversion — an automatic IRS scheme that returns excess contributions to the saver each year
new.context: Backdoor Roth is fully legal and widely used. Build Back Better (2021) would have ended it; the proposal failed in the Senate. Wealthy savers use it routinely; the IRS publishes guidance (Notice 2014-54).

rewrites.issue: Uses 'Roth IRA' and 'Traditional IRA' without teaching distinction — bumped to T4 to fit inline definition

new.question: Sell a stock for more than you paid = 'capital gain.' Held over a year = LONG-TERM (max 20%); under a year = SHORT-TERM (up to 37%). Warren Buffett's favorite holding period: 'forever.' In 2011 he told the Senate he paid a lower federal tax rate than his secretary. How does the long-term capital gains rate compare to her wage rate?
new.answer: Lower — the code rewards holding stocks over earning wages; Buffett's 15-20% investment rate beat his secretary's 25-28% wage rate
choices: Lower — the code rewards holding stocks over earning wages; Buffett's 15-20% investment rate beat his secretary's 25-28% wage rate
Higher — capital gains are taxed at 40% versus 25% on wages, making stock-holding tax-disadvantaged compared to W-2 income
Equal — federal law sets identical rates for capital and wage income to avoid distorting investment versus labor decisions
Capped — capital gains stop being taxed once income crosses $100,000, while wages continue to be taxed at all higher levels
new.context: Long-term capital gains brackets: 0%, 15%, 20%. Qualified dividends get the same low rates. Obama proposed the 'Buffett Rule' (min 30% on incomes >$1M); it never passed. The preference is durable politically.

rewrites.issue: Uses 'long-term capital gains rate' without teaching the term — bumped to T4 to fit inline definition

new.question: In 1920 Boston, Italian immigrant Charles Ponzi promised 50% returns in 45 days from international postal-coupon arbitrage. Within months ~$20M lost; his scheme collapsed. He named the category. What was the mechanism?
new.answer: Pay earlier investors with newer investors' money — no real profit; collapses when new deposits slow
choices: Pay earlier investors with newer investors' money — no real profit; collapses when new deposits slow
Steal from a corporate treasury — Ponzi siphoned from a real business he had taken over
Manipulate stock prices via insider trading — front-running customer orders on the floor
Forge counterfeit paper currency — print dollar bills on a hidden press and circulate them
new.context: Ponzi exploited international reply coupons but never executed the arbitrage. He took deposits, paid earlier investors back, pocketed the rest. Served ~14 years total. Pattern recurs: Madoff 1990s-2008, Stanford, countless smaller — same mechanics, different decade.

adds.purpose: Charles Ponzi 1920 origin — names the man behind 'Ponzi scheme'

new.question: Richard Cantillon (~1680-1734) was an Irish-French banker who personally survived John Law's Mississippi Bubble — and walked away with a fortune. His Essai sur la Nature du Commerce was published posthumously in 1755. Hayek later called him 'the first economist.' Why does the Cantillon effect carry his name?
new.answer: Cantillon first observed — having watched the Mississippi crash close-up — that new money helps whoever receives it first at the expense of late recipients
choices: Cantillon first observed — having watched the Mississippi crash close-up — that new money helps whoever receives it first at the expense of late recipients
Cantillon proved mathematically that monetary expansion is neutral — his Essai is celebrated for showing money supply changes affect all prices simultaneously
Cantillon argued paper money cannot inflate — his Essai defended John Law's scheme and is the founding text of paper-money theory in modern economics
Cantillon predicted the gold standard — his Essai was the first sustained argument that all currencies must be backed 100% by physical gold to function
new.context: Cantillon was probably murdered in his London home May 1734; case unsolved. The Essai (1755) influenced Quesnay, Turgot, Adam Smith — published 21 years before Wealth of Nations. Rothbard called it 'the first systematic treatise on economics.'

adds.purpose: Richard Cantillon biographical — the man behind the Cantillon effect

new.question: July 1850, dying of tuberculosis at 49, Frédéric Bastiat published his last pamphlet: 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen.' It opens with a broken window in a baker's shop. Why is the scenario foundational?
new.answer: The glazier's earnings are seen; what the baker would have spent on shoes is unseen — account for both
choices: The glazier's earnings are seen; what the baker would have spent on shoes is unseen — account for both
Destruction creates wealth — breaking things stimulates the economy and is therefore good policy
The shopkeeper is to blame — Bastiat criticized the baker for negligence in protecting the window
Foreign trade fixes the loss — the baker should buy windows from cheaper foreign producers
new.context: Bastiat died December 24, 1850, five months after the essay. The lesson — count what's unseen — is foundational. Modern applications: war is not stimulus, disaster spending is not gain, jobs programs trade visible work for invisible alternatives.

adds.purpose: Bastiat 1850 'That Which is Seen' essay origin

new.question: John Law (1671-1729) was a Scottish economist and gambler exiled from Britain for killing a man in a duel. In 1716 he convinced French regent Philippe d'Orléans to let him issue paper banknotes through a state-backed bank. His Mississippi Company issued shares against speculative French Louisiana profits. Shares inflated 20× through 1719, peaked early 1720, and collapsed by year-end — wiping out French savers. What did the experiment prove about paper money?
new.answer: Paper money issued faster than the productive capacity behind it inflates whatever asset it chases — shares rose 20× then collapsed, and France abandoned paper money for nearly a century
choices: Paper money issued faster than the productive capacity behind it inflates whatever asset it chases — shares rose 20× then collapsed, and France abandoned paper money for nearly a century
Paper money is structurally identical to gold — Law's experiment proved that any state-backed currency works as well as commodity money under all economic conditions
Paper money creates real wealth — Law's scheme expanded French industry permanently, and the 1720 'crash' was a brief speculative shakeout, not a fundamental failure
Paper money cannot be inflated — Law had carefully matched note issuance to Mississippi profits, and the collapse was caused by foreign speculators rather than by overissuance
new.context: Richard Cantillon personally knew Law and traded his shares — exiting with a fortune before the crash. The Mississippi + South Sea Bubbles (same year, England) were the first modern financial bubbles. Rothbard called Law 'a remarkable mixture of charlatan and prophet.' Every fiat-currency collapse since — Continental, assignats, Reichsmark, Zimbabwe, Venezuela — recapitulates Law's basic error.

adds.purpose: John Law Mississippi Bubble 1719-20 — first paper-money disaster

new.question: Ludwig von Mises published 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' in 1920 — a 36-page essay arguing socialism wasn't merely inefficient but IMPOSSIBLE. He took the strongest socialist version: a planner with perfect intentions and perfect data. Why did he say even this planner cannot run an economy?
new.answer: Without private ownership of capital goods, no prices form for them — no way to compare 'steel for railroads vs ships'; rational allocation impossible
choices: Without private ownership of capital goods, no prices form for them — no way to compare 'steel for railroads vs ships'; rational allocation impossible
Workers refuse to work — Mises argued the labor incentive problem alone makes socialism impossible, and prices would be available if motivation could be solved
Socialism requires more computing than 1920 could build — Mises argued the calculation could be performed once enough computing power existed in a future tech era
International trade isolates socialist economies — Mises argued the impossibility comes from external embargo, not from features of the socialist system itself
new.context: Mises's calculation argument is foundational to Austrian economics. Lange's 1936-37 'market socialism' attempt to refute it failed — it required real prices to feed into the central plan. The 20th century — USSR, Mao, Khmer Rouge — ran the experiment at 65-100M lives.

adds.purpose: Mises 1920 calculation argument — what the paper said

new.question: Friedrich Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' appeared in the American Economic Review in September 1945 — one of the most-cited essays of the century. Hayek argued the basic economic problem isn't how to allocate given resources optimally. What is the real problem?
new.answer: How to use knowledge that exists only in scattered, partial form across millions — knowledge no central mind possesses; the price system coordinates it
choices: How to use knowledge that exists only in scattered, partial form across millions — knowledge no central mind possesses; the price system coordinates it
How to maximize a single objective function under known resource constraints — Hayek argued the optimization problem is what economists should study using advanced math
How to predict consumer preferences using surveys — Hayek argued survey methodology was the profession's foundational tool, and prices were a secondary side issue
How to enforce international trade agreements — Hayek argued the only real economic problem is coordinating between nations, since local prices solve themselves
new.context: Hayek called the price system 'a marvel.' Example: someone in a copper mine has tacit knowledge — 'the ore is harder here' — that no central authority can collect, but the copper price transmits in summary form worldwide. Spontaneous order emerges because no one designs it. 1974 Nobel.

adds.purpose: Hayek 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' — what the AER paper argued

new.question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock published 'The Calculus of Consent' in 1962, applying economic methods — rational self-interest, marginal analysis — to politics. Before 1962, political science assumed politicians acted in 'the public interest.' What was the central claim?
new.answer: Politicians, bureaucrats, and voters are self-interested actors like businesspeople — no separate 'public-interest' motivation; political institutions need economic analysis
choices: Politicians, bureaucrats, and voters are self-interested actors like businesspeople — no separate 'public-interest' motivation; political institutions need economic analysis
Politicians act for the public interest while businesspeople act selfishly — the moral asymmetry between politics and markets justifies extensive regulation
Voters are perfectly informed and choose rationally — democratic outcomes maximize social welfare under standard assumptions of the founding model
Bureaucrats serve their agencies' missions selflessly — civil-service incentives produce socially optimal regulation without outside constraint at all
new.context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for public-choice work. The 'market failure → government intervention' argument collapses — government has its own failure modes. Public choice predicts regulatory capture (Stigler 1971), rent-seeking, the revolving door.

adds.purpose: Buchanan + Tullock 1962 — the founding moment of public choice

new.question: Bitcoin's ledger is a 'blockchain' because transactions are grouped into BLOCKS — ~10 min each, cryptographically linked. Genesis block: Jan 3, 2009. Block 709,632: Nov 14, 2021. What does 'in a block' mean?
new.answer: Bundled with ~2,000 others by a miner, sealed cryptographically, added to the ledger — undoing means redoing all later work
choices: Bundled with ~2,000 others by a miner, sealed cryptographically, added to the ledger — undoing means redoing all later work
Submitted to a private server run by Core developers — they decide which transactions to approve in chronological order daily
Emailed to every Bitcoin user worldwide — each user manually approves before the transaction counts as final between parties
Printed on a paper certificate at a Swiss Bitcoin office — physical records are the legal proof of ownership the network uses
new.context: A block has transactions, timestamp, prior-block hash, and proof-of-work. Block time averages 10 min; difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks. After ~6 confirmations (~1 hour), reversing becomes effectively impossible.

adds.purpose: Bitcoin block foundation — what kids reading 'block 709,632' need first

new.question: Every 210,000 Bitcoin blocks — about four years — the per-block reward halves. Started 50 BTC (2009); now 3.125 BTC (April 2024). Why was 'halving' built in?
new.answer: To make supply provably finite — total caps at 21M coins around year 2140
choices: To make supply provably finite — total caps at 21M coins around year 2140
To reward miners more as electricity costs rise — a built-in inflation adjustment
To let Core developers ship a new code release — every four years on coordinated dates
To match the four-year US election cycle — designed to coincide with presidential terms
new.context: Halvings: Nov 2012 (50→25), Jul 2016 (25→12.5), May 2020 (12.5→6.25), Apr 2024 (6.25→3.125). Schedule is hardcoded — no central authority can alter. Fixed-supply commitment is Bitcoin's defining property versus fiat.

adds.purpose: Bitcoin halving foundation — every ~4 years, block reward halves

new.question: FICA payroll tax is 15.3% combined: 7.65% off the employee's stub, 7.65% paid 'by the employer.' The employer half never appears on the paystub — but economists agree it ultimately comes out of wages. The combined 15.3% is the 'tax wedge.' Why is the employer half borne by the worker?
new.answer: Employers price total labor cost (wage + employer FICA) — when the tax exists, wages offered are lower by that amount; workers pay the full 15.3% invisibly
choices: Employers price total labor cost (wage + employer FICA) — when the tax exists, wages offered are lower by that amount; workers pay the full 15.3% invisibly
Employers absorb the employer half from corporate profits — workers genuinely pay only the 7.65% shown on the stub; 'wedge' framing is misleading rhetoric
Employers pass the employer half to customers as higher prices — workers pay none of it; cost falls entirely on consumers in unrelated retail transactions
Employers pay the employer half from federal subsidies — the government refunds the matching contribution, making it a pure pass-through with no real burden
new.context: The 'tax wedge' is the gap between what an employer pays to hire a worker and what the worker takes home. US ~30%; Belgium ~53%. Gruber 1997 documented employer-half shift onto wages using Chilean data. Anna earns $40,000 but her boss spent $43,060.

adds.purpose: Tax wedge foundation — employer half is hidden from the paystub
